lesson.title: Numbers With a Decimal Point: The float Type
lesson.summary: The float type represents numbers with a fractional part using binary floating point, a format that trades exactness for range and can produce small, predictable rounding errors.
lesson.body:
A float in Python represents a number with a fractional part: values like 3.14, -0.5, or 2.0. Floats exist because plenty of real quantities are not whole, such as a price in dollars and cents, a temperature reading, or the result of dividing two integers that do not divide evenly. Any numeric literal written with a decimal point, or in scientific notation like 6.02e23, is automatically treated as a float rather than an int.

Internally, Python floats are stored using a format called IEEE 754 double precision, the same standard used by nearly every mainstream programming language. This format represents numbers using binary fractions, and binary fractions cannot represent every decimal value exactly, in the same way that one third cannot be written exactly as a finite decimal in base ten. This leads to a famous and genuinely surprising trace:

x = 0.1 + 0.2
print(x)

You might expect 0.3, but Python prints 0.30000000000000004. This is not a bug in Python and not a mistake anywhere in your code; it is a direct consequence of the fact that 0.1 and 0.2 cannot be stored exactly in binary floating point, so tiny representation errors creep in and surface once you combine them. The practical lesson is to avoid comparing floats with == when checking mathematical equality, and to round explicitly, using round(x, 2) for example, before displaying a float to a user.

Floats and integers mix freely in arithmetic. Whenever an operation involves at least one float, Python promotes the result to a float, even if the other operand is an int. Consider price = 3 * 1.5: even though 3 is an integer, multiplying it by the float 1.5 produces the float 4.5. This automatic promotion is an example of implicit type conversion, covered later in this unit, and it means you rarely need to convert an int to a float by hand before doing math with it.

Choosing between int and float is a decision about what a value actually means, not just what it looks like right now. A count of items should stay an int even if you currently only have one; a measurement, an average, or anything computed through division should generally be a float, because those values are conceptually allowed to have a fractional part even when the fraction happens to equal zero.

Python floats also carry a couple of special values worth knowing about, even though you will not need them often. float("inf") represents an infinitely large value, useful as a starting point when searching for a minimum, since almost any real number will compare as smaller than it. float("nan") represents "not a number," the result you sometimes get from an undefined calculation, and it has the unusual property that it is never equal to anything, not even to itself, so nan == nan evaluates to False. Neither of these comes up in basic arithmetic, but recognizing them keeps a stray nan in your output from looking like a mysterious bug instead of a value with a name and a reason for appearing.
